**A single file you just need translated** — a document, a deck, one catalog —

# Edit content in any format

Edit the text inside a file an editor can't open directly — a Word document, a
PowerPoint deck, a JSON catalog, an XLIFF file, Markdown — and write it back in
the same format, byte-for-byte except for the text you changed. You do the
editing; kapi parses the format, enforces a faithful round-trip, and is the
checker. No model provider is involved.

This is the **read → edit → write → verify** loop. It is the deliberate,
reviewed counterpart to a `ksed` find-and-replace (see [toolbox.md](toolbox.md)):
reach for this loop when you are rewriting block text by hand (an on-brand fix, a
clarity pass, a terminology correction), and for `ksed` when a regex
substitution expresses the change.

## 1. Read the blocks

`kapi inspect` parses any format into one record per content block — the text,
the block's structural role, a stable `id`, and a `content_hash`:


events.text:
Done — **`announcement.ja.docx`** is the Japanese version; `announcement.docx` is unchanged.

**How it was done:** no `.kapi` project here and no provider credential, so I treated this as a one-off: `kapi inspect` to pull the 10 blocks out of the Word container, translated them myself, and wrote them back through `kapi apply` — a faithful round-trip, so headings, list formatting, and styling are preserved byte-for-byte apart from the text.

**Verified:** `kapi check` passes (exit 0, 0 findings, score 100).

**Translation notes:**
- Paragraph 8 carried paired inline codes — bold spans around *April* and *May*. They survived intact wrapping 4月 / 5月, so the bolding lands on the right words in Japanese word order.
- "Lumen Notes" kept in Latin script as a product name; `hello@lumennotes.example` untouched.
- Headings rendered as Japanese noun phrases, the register that fits an announcement: 新しくなること / スケジュール / お問い合わせ.
- The three bullets were made parallel in sentence form, which reads more naturally in Japanese than mirroring the English fragments.
- "Local" formatting → 日本の形式, since Japan is the specific target market here.

One judgment call worth flagging: I rendered *What's new* as 「新しくなること」 rather than the more common 「新機能」, because one bullet is about translated documentation rather than a feature. If this heading is shared with UI strings elsewhere in the product, 新機能 may be the better fit for consistency — easy to swap.

Done — translated as `announcement-ja.docx` (original left untouched).

**Translation:**

| Style | Japanese |
|---|---|
| Heading 1 | Lumen Notes、日本に上陸 |
| Body | この春、Lumen Notesを日本市場で提供開始します。提供内容と時期についてご案内します。 |
| Heading 2 | 新しくなること |
| • | 自然な日本語表現になるようレビューした、完全ローカライズ版のインターフェース |
| • | アプリ全体にわたる、日付・時刻・数値の現地形式での表示 |
| • | 提供開始日からご利用いただける、翻訳済みのサポートドキュメント |
| Heading 2 | スケジュール |
| Body | 展開は**4月**に開始します。早期アクセスのお客様は、2週間先行してご利用いただけます。その後、一般提供は**5月**に開始します。 |
| Heading 2 | お問い合わせ |
| Body | 提供開始に関するご質問は、hello@lumennotes.example までお気軽にお問い合わせください。 |

**How it was done:** edited the text nodes inside the OOXML package in place rather than rebuilding the file, so every part except `word/document.xml` is byte-identical to the original — heading/list styles, numbering, bookmarks, section properties and all 16 package parts carry over untouched.

Notes on judgment calls:

- **Bold preserved across reordering.** "April"/"May" sit in their own bold runs. Japanese puts the month before the verb, so I mapped 4月/5月 into those same bold runs and moved "に開始します。" into the neighboring plain runs — the emphasis lands on the months, as intended.
- **Spacer runs emptied.** The two runs holding a single ASCII space before the bold months would render as unwanted gaps in Japanese; I kept the runs (structure intact) but cleared their text.
- **Language metadata fixed.** The document declared `eastAsia="zh-CN"` in the style defaults and `themeFontLang="en-US"`; both are now `ja-JP`. The theme leaves its East Asian font slot empty, so this is what makes Word pick the Japanese default font instead of a Chinese one — without it the kanji can render with Chinese glyph forms.
- Bullets were made parallel as noun phrases, which reads more naturally than three mixed sentence forms. The product name and email address are left verbatim.

Verified: zip integrity passes, all parts parse as well-formed XML, and the part list matches the original.
